sections.html: Time zones let different places use clock times suited to their part of the day. As Earth turns, your afternoon can be a distant friend’s morning. Someone gets breakfast while you are washing the lunch dishes.
sections.title: Your afternoon can be someone else’s morning

sections.html:
Time-zone boundaries bend because governments choose clock rules. Towns or regions may share a time for convenience rather than follow a neat stripe of longitude.

IANA records these decisions. A place’s position helps explain its daylight, but does not determine its clock on its own.
sections.title: Why aren’t time zones straight stripes?

sections.html:
UTC is a common reference for comparing clocks. An offset is the difference from that reference.

At 12 noon UTC, UTC+2 shows 14:00: two hours ahead. UTC−3 shows 09:00: three hours behind.
sections.title: UTC is a shared starting clock

sections.html: In our made-up example, City A uses UTC+2 and City B uses UTC−3. From 14:00 in City A, go back two hours to noon UTC, then three more to 09:00 in City B.
sections.title: Follow one call, step by step

sections.title: Three clocks at the same moment

sections.html:
Some places change clocks for daylight saving time; others do not. A time zone includes those rules, not just today’s offset.

For a real call or journey, check the city and the date in a calendar or world-clock tool. Yesterday’s difference may not apply all year.
